OAuth setup for your app

Source: vignettes/oauth-setup.Rmd
oauth-setup.Rmd

OAuth lets your Shiny app query data on behalf of the person who signed in. The database still decides what that person may read. Start with your database guide for a complete app; use this page to understand the settings it asks you to collect.

What the settings mean

Setting Meaning
Client ID The sign-in service’s identifier for your Shiny app
Client secret The app’s credential, stored on the Shiny server
Redirect URI The exact address where the browser returns after sign-in
Issuer The sign-in service’s URL, identifying who issues tokens
Scope A permission the app asks the person to approve
Audience The database or API the access token is intended for
Database role The permissions the database applies after checking the token

The guides use http://localhost:8100 as the callback for apps you run in R. The packaged Docker demos use http://localhost:18100. Register the exact value, including any path and trailing slash. Use your app’s HTTPS address when deploying.

Save credentials in R

Open the environment file for your app project:

file.edit(".Renviron")

Add the values from the registration, as shown in the backend guide:

OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID=your-client-id
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret

Restart R, then Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID") should return the ID. Keep .Renviron out of Git. On a hosting service, set the same environment variables in the app’s settings. The secret belongs on the server.

Register a Microsoft Entra app

Azure SQL, Fabric and Azure PostgreSQL use Microsoft Entra. Start in the Entra admin center, under App registrations. Create a registration in your organization’s tenant, then copy Application (client) ID and Directory (tenant) ID from its overview. Under Authentication, add a Web platform with http://localhost:8100. Under Certificates & secrets, create a client secret and copy its Value before leaving. Save the tenant ID as OAUTHDB_TENANT_ID. Microsoft’s registration instructions describe the available account types.

Under API permissions, add the backend’s delegated permission: the app acts as the signed-in person. SQL uses Azure SQL Database’s user_impersonation; Azure PostgreSQL uses Azure OSSRDBMS Database access. Fabric API calls need the permissions listed in the Fabric guide. An administrator may need to grant consent or allow the application.

Database access is a separate step: the administrator must also create or grant the person’s database identity. A successful Microsoft login doesn’t give a user access to a table.

Use Keycloak with a self-hosted database

Keycloak is an open-source sign-in service you can host beside your database. The local demos already register an app, create accounts and configure database audiences. Copy their files with oauth_db_demo(action = "files") to inspect an example.

For your own realm, create an OpenID Connect client in Keycloak’s Clients screen. Enable the authorization-code (Standard) flow and PKCE S256; enter your exact Shiny callback under valid redirect URIs. For a server app with client authentication enabled, copy its secret from the credentials tab. The demos use a confidential client with a public demo secret. Use a secret belonging to your own registration when deploying.

Find the issuer in the realm’s OpenID configuration. It normally looks like https://login.example.org/realms/reporting. The discovery document also lists jwks_uri, where the database can fetch public signing keys. Use client scopes and protocol mappers to include the database audience and the claims required by its guide. Configure the database to trust those keys and map verified identities to database permissions. See Keycloak’s administration guide.

Check the database accepts the token

Browser sign-in alone isn’t enough. The database must trust the token’s issuer and signing keys, accept its audience, and recognize its identity or role claim. The app sends an access token to the database; an ID token describes the login and serves a different purpose.

If login works but queries fail, compare the registration’s audience, scopes and claim mapping with the database configuration. Check database grants and network access next. Keep tokens and secrets out of logs.

For a client that needs several APIs, token targets obtain a separate token for each resource. See Authentication and sessions after your first query works.
